comparisons.peer_topic: Minimum CET1 Capital Ratio Requirements and Buffers
comparisons.peer_summary: To avoid restrictions on capital distributions and bonus payments, the Corporation must meet CET1 capital ratio requirements including buffers and G-SIB surcharges, requiring minimum ratios of 10.0% from Jan 1 to Sep 30, 2024, and 10.7% (Standardized) or 10.0% (Advanced) from Oct 1, 2024. These requirements must be comprised solely of CET1 capital.
comparisons.comparison: While MS monitors the ongoing Basel III Endgame and G-SIB surcharge proposals, BAC discloses its current binding minimum CET1 capital ratio requirements which incorporate buffers and G-SIB surcharges. BAC specifies that for the period from January 1, 2024, through September 30, 2024, the minimum requirement was 10.0%, effective October 1, 2024, requirements increased to 10.7% under the Standardized approach, reflecting the application of the regulatory frameworks MS is monitoring.

sentences.text: On July 27, 2023, U.S. banking agencies proposed revisions to risk-based capital and related standards applicable to us and our U.S. Bank Subsidiaries ("Basel III Endgame Proposal").
We continue to monitor developments related to this rulemaking as well as the proposed revisions to the G-SIB capital surcharge framework.

In order to avoid restrictions on capital distributions and discretionary bonus payments to executive officers, the Corporation must meet risk-based capital ratio requirements that include a capital conservation buffer of 2.5 percent (under the Advanced approaches only), an SCB (under the Standardized approach only), plus any applicable countercyclical capital buffer and a global systemically important bank (G-SIB) surcharge.

For the period from January 1, 2024 through September 30, 2024, the Corporation's minimum CET1 capital ratio requirements were 10.0 percent under both the Standardized approach and the Advanced approaches.
Effective October 1, 2024, the Corporation's minimum CET1 requirements were 10.7 percent under the Standardized approach and 10.0 percent under the Advanced approaches.

comparisons.peer_topic: G-SIB Surcharge Calculation and Future Increase
comparisons.peer_summary: The Corporation calculates its G-SIB surcharge annually using two methods and is subject to the higher result; the surcharge is expected to increase to 3.5% from 3.0% on January 1, 2027, unless the December 31, 2025 calculation yields a lower value. At December 31, 2024, the Corporation's CET1 capital ratio of 11.9% under the Standardized approach exceeded its requirement.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures concern the G-SIB surcharge calculation methodology and future expectations. MS monitors the proposed revisions to the G-SIB capital surcharge framework, while BAC details its current calculation using two methods (Method 1 and Method 2) and notes that the surcharge is expected to increase to 3.5% from 3.0% on January 1, 2027, unless the December 31, 2025 calculation yields a lower value.

sentences.text: We continue to monitor developments related to this rulemaking as well as the proposed revisions to the G-SIB capital surcharge framework.
The Corporation is required to calculate its G-SIB surcharge on an annual basis under two methods and is subject to the higher of the resulting two surcharges.

The Corporation's G-SIB surcharge, which is higher under Method 2, is expected to increase to 3.5 percent from 3.0 percent on January 1, 2027, unless its surcharge calculated as of December 31, 2025 is lower than 3.5 percent.

comparisons.peer_topic: U.S. Basel III Finalization Proposal Details
comparisons.peer_summary: In July 2023, U.S. regulators released the U.S. Basel III proposal to amend the risk-based capital framework, which includes replacing the Advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach for calculating risk-weighted assets and applying the stress capital buffer to both the expanded risk-based and Standardized approaches.
comparisons.comparison: Both Bank of America (MS) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM) monitor the same U.S. regulatory proposals introduced in July 2023 regarding Basel III capital standards and G-SIB surcharges. MS discloses it continues to monitor these developments, while JPM details the specific components of the proposal, such as replacing the Advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach for calculating risk-weighted assets.

sentences.text: On July 27, 2023, U.S. banking agencies proposed revisions to risk-based capital and related standards applicable to us and our U.S. Bank Subsidiaries ("Basel III Endgame Proposal").
We continue to monitor developments related to this rulemaking as well as the proposed revisions to the G-SIB capital surcharge framework.

In July 2023, the Federal Reserve, the OCC and the FDIC released a proposal to amend the risk-based capital framework, entitled "Regulatory capital rule: Amendments applicable to large banking organizations and to banking organizations with significant trading activity", which is referred to in this Form 10-K as the "U.S. Basel III proposal".
Under this proposal, changes to the framework would include replacement of the Advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach for the calculation of RWA.

comparisons.peer_summary: In July 2023, the Federal Reserve proposed amendments to the GSIB surcharge calculation, including averaging methods, reduced surcharge increments, and technical changes to the Method 2 calculation, which would revise risk-based capital requirements for the Firm and other U.S. GSIBs.
comparisons.comparison: Both MS and JPM reference the July 2023 proposal to amend the G-SIB capital surcharge framework. MS lists this as a parallel development it monitors, while JPM elaborates on the proposal's specific changes, including the shift to annual GSIB surcharge averaging based on quarterly calculations and the reduction of surcharge increments from 50 basis points to 10 basis points.

sentences.text: We continue to monitor developments related to this rulemaking as well as the proposed revisions to the G-SIB capital surcharge framework.
In July 2023, the Federal Reserve released a proposal to amend the calculation of the GSIB surcharge.
The proposal would also reduce surcharge increments from 50 bps to 10 bps and includes other technical amendments to the "Method 2" calculation.
